question.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=4xy-2{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨1,1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4,4⟩,$ respectively.
question.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=4xy-2{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨1,1,2⟩$ and $b=⟨2,4,4⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,4,4)-f(1,1,2) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,4,4⟩-⟨1,1,2⟩) \\ 0-(-4) & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩ \\ 4 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨4y,4x,-4z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨4{c}_{2},4{c}_{1},-4{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩ \\ 4 & =⟨4{c}_{2},4{c}_{1},-4{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨1,3,2⟩ \\ 4 & =4{c}_{2}+12{c}_{1}-8{c}_{3} \\ 1 & =3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{1} & =\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z-2}{2} \\ x-1 & =\frac{y-1}{3}=\frac{z-2}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=t+1,\,y=3t+1,\,z=2t+2,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=t+1,\,{c}_{2}=3t+1,\,{c}_{3}=2t+2.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $3{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}-2{c}_{3}=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3(t+1)+(3t+1)-2(2t+2) & =1 \\ 3t+3+3t+1-4t-4 & =1 \\ 2t & =1 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =\frac{1}{2}+1=\frac{3}{2}, \\ {c}_{2} & =3(\frac{1}{2})+1=\frac{5}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =2(\frac{1}{2})+2=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2},3).$
